records.q1: What are the transparency obligations for general-purpose AI model providers under the EU AI Act?

records.gold_answer: Providers of general-purpose AI models must draw up and keep up-to-date technical documentation (Article 53(1)(a)), make information and documentation available to downstream providers (Article 53(1)(b)), establish a copyright compliance policy respecting Directive (EU) 2019/790 (Article 53(1)(c)), and publish a publicly available summary of training content (Article 53(1)(d)).

turn1.answer: Every provider of a general-purpose AI model owes four duties under Article 53(1): technical documentation covering the model's training and testing process and evaluation results, in accordance with Annex XI, made available to the AI Office and national competent authorities; information and documentation for downstream providers integrating the model, in accordance with Annex XII; a copyright policy complying with Union law; and a publicly available summary of the content used to train the model. Article 53(2) exempts a model released under a free and open-source licence with publicly available weights, architecture and usage information from the Annex XI documentation and Annex XII downstream-information duties only, leaving the copyright policy and training-data summary in place, and this carve-out does not apply once the model is classified as carrying systemic risk. A model is classified as carrying systemic risk under Article 51 where it has high-impact capabilities, presumed above cumulative training compute of 10^25 floating-point operations, or where the Commission so designates it. A provider of a systemic-risk model owes, in addition to the Article 53 duties, the Article 55 obligations of state-of-the-art model evaluation including documented adversarial testing, assessment and mitigation of systemic risks at Union level, reporting of serious incidents to the AI Office without undue delay, and cybersecurity protection for the model and its physical infrastructure. Where the model is made available within a system that interacts directly with natural persons or generates synthetic content, the provider also owes the Article 50 transparency duties of ensuring persons are informed they are interacting with an AI system and marking synthetic output in a machine-readable, detectable format as artificially generated or manipulated.

turn3.answer: Every provider of a general-purpose AI model must draw up and keep up to date technical documentation of the model, including its training and testing process and evaluation results, in the form set out in Annex XI, and supply information and documentation to downstream providers integrating the model as specified in Annex XII, along with a copyright policy and a publicly available summary of the content used for training under Article 53. Article 53(2) exempts a model released under a free and open-source licence with publicly available parameters from the Annex XI and Annex XII duties, though the copyright policy and training-data summary duties still apply to it. Where the model is classified as carrying systemic risk under Article 51, on the presumption that cumulative training compute exceeds 10^25 floating point operations, the open-source exemption falls away and Article 55 adds model evaluation including documented adversarial testing, assessment and mitigation of systemic risks at Union level, reporting of serious incidents to the AI Office, and cybersecurity protection of the model and its physical infrastructure. A provider may rely on a code of practice under Article 56 to demonstrate compliance with Articles 53 and 55 pending a harmonised standard. Where the model is made available within a system that interacts directly with natural persons or generates synthetic content, the provider additionally bears the Article 50 duties to disclose the AI interaction and to mark synthetic output in a machine-readable, detectable format.

records.gold_answer: Under Article 9, a risk management system must be established, implemented, documented, and maintained as a continuous iterative process throughout the entire lifecycle of a high-risk AI system. It requires identifying and analysing known and foreseeable risks, evaluating risks that may emerge during use, and adopting targeted risk mitigation and control measures.

turn1.answer: A risk management system for a high-risk AI system must be established, implemented, documented and maintained as a continuous iterative process throughout the system's lifecycle under Article 9(1). It must identify and analyse known and reasonably foreseeable risks to health, safety or fundamental rights under Article 9(2)(a), and estimate and evaluate risks that may emerge from use in accordance with the intended purpose and from reasonably foreseeable misuse under Article 9(2)(b). Article 9(4) requires the provider to give due consideration to the effects and possible interactions arising from the combined application of the high-risk requirements, so as to minimise risks effectively while achieving an appropriate balance in implementing the measures taken to comply with them. Article 9(5) requires the system to be tested to identify the most appropriate and targeted risk management measures and to ensure it performs consistently for its intended purpose, and Article 9(6) requires that residual risk for each hazard, and the overall residual risk, be judged acceptable and communicated to the deployer.

turn3.answer: Article 9 requires the provider to establish, implement, document and maintain a risk management system as a continuous iterative process planned and run throughout the entire lifecycle of the high-risk AI system, with regular systematic review and updating. It comprises identifying and analysing the known and reasonably foreseeable risks the system can pose to health, safety or fundamental rights when used as intended, estimating and evaluating the risks that may emerge under conditions of reasonably foreseeable misuse, evaluating other risks arising from post-market monitoring data, and adopting appropriate and targeted risk management measures to address the identified risks. Article 9(4) requires that these measures give due consideration to the combined effects of the requirements applied together, so as to minimise risks more effectively while achieving an appropriate balance in implementing the measures. Article 9(5) requires testing of the high-risk system to identify the most appropriate and targeted risk management measures and to ensure consistent performance for its intended purpose, and Article 9(6) requires that residual risk from each hazard and the overall residual risk be judged acceptable and communicated to the deployer.

records.gold_answer: Under Article 5(1)(h), real-time remote biometric identification systems in publicly accessible spaces for law enforcement purposes are prohibited, subject to strictly defined exceptions such as targeted search for kidnapping or human trafficking victims, prevention of specific and imminent terrorist threats, or localization of suspects of serious criminal offences.

turn1.answer: Prohibited, subject to narrow exceptions, under Article 5. The use of "real-time" remote biometric identification systems in publicly accessible spaces for the purposes of law enforcement is banned unless strictly necessary for one of three objectives: the targeted search for specific victims of abduction, trafficking or sexual exploitation and the search for missing persons, the prevention of a specific, substantial and imminent threat to life or physical safety or a genuine and present or foreseeable terrorist threat, or the localisation or identification of a person suspected of a qualifying serious offence. Outside law enforcement use in publicly accessible spaces, or where none of these three objectives and their strict necessity condition is met, the prohibition applies in full. The provision is a ban on the specified use, not a ban on the underlying technology as such., and it also does not extend to remote biometric identification carried out in non-publicly-accessible spaces or for purposes other than law enforcement, which fall to be assessed under the other provisions of the Regulation.

turn3.answer: The use of real-time remote biometric identification in publicly accessible spaces is prohibited under Article 5(1)(h), unless strictly necessary for one of the objectives listed in that provision.

records.gold_answer: Under Article 26, deployers of high-risk AI systems must take appropriate technical and organisational measures to ensure they use such systems in accordance with the instructions for use, assign human oversight to individuals with necessary competence and training, monitor operation for risks, maintain automatically generated logs, and inform workers and representatives where applicable.

turn1.answer: Article 26 sets out the deployer's obligations for a high-risk AI system across several paragraphs. The deployer must use the system in accordance with the instructions for use (Article 26(1)) and assign human oversight to natural persons who have the necessary competence, training, authority and support (Article 26(2)). Where the deployer exercises control over input data, it must ensure that data is relevant and sufficiently representative in view of the system's intended purpose (Article 26(4)). The deployer must monitor the system's operation on the basis of the instructions for use, inform the provider of serious incidents, and, where use in accordance with the instructions may result in the system presenting a risk, inform the provider or distributor and the relevant market surveillance authority without undue delay and suspend use of the system (Article 26(5)). It must retain the automatically generated logs under its control for a period appropriate to the system's intended purpose, of at least six months, unless other applicable Union or national law provides otherwise (Article 26(6)). An employer deploying the system at the workplace must inform workers' representatives and the affected workers before putting the system into service (Article 26(7)). A deployer that is a public authority or a Union institution, body, office or agency must comply with the registration obligations and must not use a system that has not been registered (Article 26(8)). Where applicable, the deployer must use the information provided to it to fulfil its own data protection impact assessment obligation (Article 26(9)). A deployer of an Annex III high-risk system that makes or assists in making decisions about natural persons must inform those persons that they are subject to the system's use (Article 26(11)). Finally, the deployer must cooperate with the relevant competent authorities in any action those authorities take in relation to the system (Article 26(12)).

turn3.answer: Article 26 sets six core duties for the deployer of a high-risk AI system. The deployer must use the system in accordance with the instructions for use (Article 26(1)), assign human oversight to natural persons who have the necessary competence, training and authority (Article 26(2)), and, to the extent it exercises control over input data, ensure that input data is relevant and sufficiently representative for the system's intended purpose (Article 26 point on input data control). The deployer must monitor the system's operation on the basis of the instructions for use and inform the provider of serious incidents (Article 26(5)), and it must retain the automatically generated logs under its control for a period appropriate to the system's intended purpose, of at least six months unless other Union or national law provides otherwise (Article 26(6)). A deployer that is an employer must inform affected workers and their representatives before putting the system into service at the workplace (Article 26(7)), and every deployer must cooperate with the competent market surveillance authorities in any action they take regarding the system (Article 26). Deployers that are financial institutions subject to Union financial services internal-governance requirements satisfy the Article 26(5) monitoring duty and the Article 26(6) log-retention duty by complying with the governance arrangements required under that financial services legislation.

records.gold_answer: An AI system referred to in Annex III is not high-risk if it does not pose a significant risk of harm to health, safety, or fundamental rights and meets at least one condition in Article 6(3): performing a narrow procedural task, improving human activity results, detecting decision patterns, or preparatory tasks. Profiling always precludes the exemption.

turn1.answer: Under Article 6(3), an Annex III system is not high-risk where it poses no significant risk of harm and meets one of four conditions: it performs a narrow procedural task, it improves the result of a previously completed human activity, it detects decision-making patterns or deviations without replacing or influencing the human assessment, or it performs a preparatory task. Under Article 6(3), this exception never applies where the system profiles natural persons. The provider must document the assessment before placing the system on the market and register it under Article 49(2).

turn3.answer: Under Article 6(3), an Annex III system is not high-risk where it poses no significant risk of harm and meets one of four conditions: it performs a narrow procedural task, it improves the result of a previously completed human activity, it detects decision-making patterns or deviations without replacing or influencing the human assessment, or it performs a preparatory task. Under Article 6(3), this exception never applies where the system profiles natural persons. The provider must document the assessment before placing the system on the market and register it under Article 49(2).
